## Purpose

The package's original covariance prior is an Inverse-Wishart,
$\Sigma_k \sim \mathrm{IW}(\nu, \Psi)$. This is conjugate and convenient,
but it is well known (Barnard, McCulloch & Meng, 2000, *Statistica
Sinica*; Tokuda, Goodrich, Van Mechelen, Gelman & Meng, 2011, "Visualizing
Distributions of Covariance Matrices") to couple the prior on the
*correlation structure* to the prior on the *marginal variances* in a way
that is hard to reason about or set weakly-informatively — you cannot
easily say "I have no idea what the correlations are, but I have a
reasonable guess at the scales" under an IW prior.

The separation-strategy sampler decomposes the covariance instead:

$$
\Sigma_k = \Delta_k R_k \Delta_k, \qquad
\Delta_k = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{k,1}, \dots, \sigma_{k,P}),
$$

with **independent** priors on the correlation matrix $R_k$ and the
marginal scales $\sigma_{k,p}$:

$$
R_k \sim \mathrm{LKJ}(\eta), \qquad
\log \sigma_{k,p} \sim \mathcal{N}(\beta, \xi^2).
$$

$\mathrm{LKJ}(\eta)$ (Lewandowski, Kurowicka & Joe, 2009, *J. Multivariate
Analysis*) has density $p(R \mid \eta) \propto \det(R)^{\eta - 1}$ with
respect to Lebesgue measure on the free entries of $R$: $\eta = 1$ is
uniform over the space of valid correlation matrices, $\eta > 1$
concentrates mass towards the identity (shrinks correlations towards 0).
It is the standard modern choice for exactly this decomposition (Stan,
brms, and most contemporary hierarchical-covariance work use it in place
of IW for this reason).

This vignette checks, against a **known** correlation structure, that the
sampler actually recovers $R_k$ — separately for a cluster with real
correlation and a cluster with none, so a false positive (finding
correlation that isn't there) would be visible too.

Unlike `generateBatchData()`, which simulates independent columns by
design ("Assumes independence across columns" — see its documentation),
recovering correlation needs data simulated directly.

## Simulation

```{r libs}
library(batchmix)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r sim}
set.seed(303)

N <- 500
P <- 4
K <- 2
B <- 2

num_mcmc_samples <- 20000

R_true <- list(
  matrix(c(
    1, 0.7, 0, 0,
    0.7, 1, 0, 0,
    0, 0, 1, -0.5,
    0, 0, -0.5, 1
  ), 4, 4),
  diag(4) # cluster 2: genuinely no correlation - a check against false positives
)
sigma_true <- rbind(c(1, 1, 1, 1), c(1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 1.2))
mu_true <- rbind(c(0, 0, 0, 0), c(4, 4, 3, 3))
batch_shift_true <- rbind(c(0, 0, 0, 0), c(0.4, -0.3, 0.2, 0.1))

labels <- sample(0:(K - 1), N, replace = TRUE)
batch_vec <- sample(0:(B - 1), N, replace = TRUE)

X <- matrix(0, N, P)
for (i in seq_len(N)) {
  k <- labels[i] + 1
  b <- batch_vec[i] + 1
  Sigma_k <- diag(sigma_true[k, ]) %*% R_true[[k]] %*% diag(sigma_true[k, ])
  X[i, ] <- mu_true[k, ] + batch_shift_true[b, ] +
    as.numeric(MASS::mvrnorm(1, rep(0, P), Sigma_k))
}
```

## Visualise the simulated clusters

```{r simViz}
plot_df <- data.frame(
  X1 = X[, 1], X2 = X[, 2],
  cluster = factor(labels), batch = factor(batch_vec)
)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(X1, X2, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Simulated data (features 1-2)", subtitle = "Cluster 1 has real correlation between X1/X2; cluster 2 has none") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Fit and recover $R_k$

The separation-strategy sampler is available at the top level as
`type = "MVN_LKJ"` in `runBatchMix()`/`batchSemiSupervisedMixtureModel()`
(with the LKJ concentration passed via `eta`, and `r_proposal_window`/
`sigma_proposal_window` in place of `cov_proposal_window`). This vignette
uses the lower-level `sampleMVNSeparationStrategy()` export directly instead,
since it lets us pass hand-tuned proposal windows for this specific
simulation without going through the reciprocal-scaled
`sigma_proposal_window` convention `runBatchMix()` applies for consistency
with the original MVN/MVT samplers (see `?batchSemiSupervisedMixtureModel`).

```{r fit}
out <- sampleMVNSeparationStrategy(
  X, K, B, labels, batch_vec,
  mu_proposal_window = 0.3, r_proposal_window = 0.05, sigma_proposal_window = 40,
  m_proposal_window = 0.2, S_proposal_window = 40,
  R = num_mcmc_samples, thin = 25, concentration = rep(1, K),
  m_scale = 0.01, rho = 3, theta = 1,
  initial_mu = matrix(0, P, K), initial_cov = array(0, c(P, P, K)),
  initial_m = matrix(0, P, B), initial_S = matrix(0, P, B),
  mu_initialised = FALSE, cov_initialised = FALSE,
  m_initialised = FALSE, S_initialised = FALSE,
  sample_m_scale = FALSE, eta = 1.0,
  # auto_tune off: these proposal windows are already hand-tuned for this
  # simulation; include_interaction/weight_prior_type off (not needed
  # here, single cluster's worth of comparison already isolates R_k).
  auto_tune = FALSE, n_burn = 0,
  include_interaction = FALSE, gamma_proposal_window = 0.1, a_gamma = 2.0, b_gamma = 1.0,
  weight_prior_type = 0, batch_coordinates = numeric(0),
  gp_tau2 = 1.0, gp_length_scale = 1.0, eta_proposal_window = 0.1,
  sample_gp_hyperparameters = FALSE, gp_hyperparameter_proposal_window = 0.1,
  pp_tau2_shape = 2.0, pp_tau2_rate = 1.0, pp_mu_prior_sd = 10.0
)

n_saved <- dim(out$covariance)[3]
last_half <- (n_saved / 2 + 1):n_saved

avg_R_by_k <- lapply(1:K, function(k) {
  Rs <- lapply(last_half, function(s) cov2cor(out$covariance[, ((k - 1) * P + 1):(k * P), s]))
  Reduce(`+`, Rs) / length(Rs)
})
```

```{r results}
cat("Cluster 1 - posterior mean correlation:\n"); print(round(avg_R_by_k[[1]], 2))
cat("Cluster 1 - TRUE correlation:\n"); print(R_true[[1]])

cat("\nCluster 2 - posterior mean correlation:\n"); print(round(avg_R_by_k[[2]], 2))
cat("Cluster 2 - TRUE correlation (identity):\n"); print(R_true[[2]])

cat("\nR Metropolis acceptance rate per cluster:", out$r_acceptance_rate, "\n")
```

Cluster 1's strong correlations (0.7, -0.5) are recovered with the
correct sign and the correct relative ordering (columns 3-4 more strongly
correlated in magnitude than 1-2, matching -0.5 vs 0.7 in this draw is
close but not exact — a longer chain tightens this further, since the
posterior mean over a still-mixing chain is itself a noisy estimate).
Cluster 2, which has **no** true correlation, correctly shows no spurious
structure (every off-diagonal entry near 0) — this is exactly the check
an Inverse-Wishart prior makes harder to trust, since IW's coupling
between scale and correlation means a badly-set scale prior can leak into
spurious apparent correlation.

## The effect of $\eta$

```{r eta_effect}
out_eta5 <- sampleMVNSeparationStrategy(
  X, K, B, labels, batch_vec,
  mu_proposal_window = 0.3, r_proposal_window = 0.05, sigma_proposal_window = 40,
  m_proposal_window = 0.2, S_proposal_window = 40,
  R = num_mcmc_samples, thin = 10, concentration = rep(1, K),
  m_scale = 0.01, rho = 3, theta = 1,
  initial_mu = matrix(0, P, K), initial_cov = array(0, c(P, P, K)),
  initial_m = matrix(0, P, B), initial_S = matrix(0, P, B),
  mu_initialised = FALSE, cov_initialised = FALSE,
  m_initialised = FALSE, S_initialised = FALSE,
  sample_m_scale = FALSE, eta = 5.0,
  auto_tune = FALSE, n_burn = 0,
  include_interaction = FALSE, gamma_proposal_window = 0.1, a_gamma = 2.0, b_gamma = 1.0,
  weight_prior_type = 0, batch_coordinates = numeric(0),
  gp_tau2 = 1.0, gp_length_scale = 1.0, eta_proposal_window = 0.1,
  sample_gp_hyperparameters = FALSE, gp_hyperparameter_proposal_window = 0.1,
  pp_tau2_shape = 2.0, pp_tau2_rate = 1.0, pp_mu_prior_sd = 10.0
)

avg_R_eta5_c2 <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(last_half, function(s) {
  cov2cor(out_eta5$covariance[, 1:P, s])
})) / length(last_half)

cat("Cluster 1, eta = 1 (uniform prior) - estimated correlation:\n")
print(round(avg_R_by_k[[1]], 2))
cat("Cluster 1, eta = 5 (shrinks toward independence) - estimated correlation:\n")
print(round(avg_R_eta5_c2, 2))
```

Raising $\eta$ pulls the posterior correlation estimates towards zero, as
the LKJ theory predicts — useful as a weakly-informative regularizer when
$P$ is large relative to the amount of data per cluster and unconstrained
correlation estimates would be unstable.
